Mr. Kuroda, your customer in Turin was very convincing. But your list price is still fifteen percent above the other finalist.
I'm glad the call went well. Fifteen percent is a lot. If you sign a multi-year deal, we will reduce the fee by eight percent.
Eight is not fifteen. Can you match their price?
We can't match it, but there is some wiggle room. If you pay annually, we'll throw in the training for your finance team.
That is a nice sweetener. And what happens if we only sign for one year?
If you sign for one year, we will keep the list price. The discount comes with the three years.
Then meet me halfway. Three years, the training, and twelve percent.
I can do ten, not twelve. If we do ten percent, will Giulia sign by Friday?

What can you give us in return?

The first discount you give is the most important one, because it teaches the buyer how you negotiate. If you give it for free, the buyer will ask for more. So my first rule is simple: never give, always trade. Put the condition first and the gift second. If you sign for three years, we will reduce the price. If you pay annually, we will throw in the training. My second rule: make the first concession small. If you start with twenty percent, the buyer will think your list price was never real. My third rule: when the buyer asks you to meet halfway, do not say yes at once. Ask a question first. If we do that, will you sign this week?

I buy software for a living, and I ask for a discount in the first meeting, every time, even when the price is fair. I want to see how much wiggle room the seller has. Last month, one seller gave me fifteen percent in the first minute. I thanked him, and then I asked for more, because now I knew his list price was not serious. Another seller said: if you commit to a multi-year deal, we can do eight percent. I asked for ten. She said: if you sign by Friday, we will do ten. That was the deal I signed. She gave me something, but every time she asked for something in return.
